analysis.one_liner: Moves most interstate consumer class actions from state courts into federal courts.
analysis.headline: The House Judiciary Committee approved the bill 17-12 and the Rules Committee set it up for floor debate, but the House never voted before the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let corporations move most class actions filed against them out of state courts and into federal courts, where it is much harder to get a class certified and cases are more often thrown out. Any single defendant — or even one unnamed class member — could force the move, at any stage of the case. Class actions are how ordinary people recover small amounts (a few dollars each) from hidden fees, defective products, or unpaid wages, so the shift would have caused many of those cases to die. The House committee approved it, but the full House never voted before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Large corporate defendants facing consumer class actions — insurers, banks, product and drug manufacturers — gain the right to move those cases out of state courts and into federal court, where judges certify fewer classes and settlement pressure is weaker. Corporate defense lawyers also gain work; plaintiffs' firms lose it.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Corporate defendants facing consumer class actions

how_it_helps.text: Grants federal courts jurisdiction over any interstate class action, no matter how small the individual claims — letting corporate defendants escape state courts, where classes are more often certified and the pressure to settle is strongest.

Lets any single defendant move a class action to federal court without the consent of the other defendants, and even lets one unnamed class member force removal — before or after a class has been certified.
As introduced, it also repealed the one-year deadline for moving a case to federal court, so a defendant could wait years and then pull the case out of state court.

The committee version was softened to defuse objections: judges would be directed to keep out cases where most class members and defendants share one state, could keep out small cases (under $1 million or fewer than 100 members), securities class actions were carved out, and a case sent back to state court would keep its deadlines paused for the plaintiffs.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers and workers with small-dollar claims — the class members themselves — plus the state courts that lose jurisdiction over these cases and the plaintiffs' firms that bring them. The cost shows up as unrecovered losses when class actions stall or die in federal court.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers and workers with small-dollar claims

drawbacks.text: The class action is the only practical way to recover small losses — a few dollars each from a hidden fee or a defective product — because no lawyer can profitably take a single small claim. Federal courts certify fewer classes than state courts, so shifting these cases to the federal system would have caused many legitimate claims to disappear.

The removal rights are sweeping: any one defendant, or even one unnamed class member, could pull a case into federal court at any stage — before or after a class was certified — giving corporate defendants an easy route out of the state forum.

The strongest good-faith argument for the bill: federal courts would apply one consistent set of procedures nationwide instead of leaving defendants at the mercy of a few plaintiff-friendly state courts. The committee tried to answer critics by directing judges to keep out small and same-state cases, carving out securities class actions, and ordering a study of the effect on federal court workloads.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits of this bill ran to corporate defendants; the costs ran to consumers. The safeguards added in committee — abstention for small and same-state cases, the securities carve-out, tolling on remand — narrowed the reach but left the core intact: defendants could move large interstate class actions into the forum where they are most likely to win. Individually these cases involve small amounts, but aggregated across millions of class members the money at stake is large, and the class action would remain the only realistic remedy for small-dollar harm.

outcome.mechanism: The House never got to a floor vote — the bill was sitting ready for debate when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999, and it died.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Hyde of Illinois, the House Judiciary chairman, introduced the bill on May 5, 1998, joined by five other original sponsors including Rep. Bill McCollum.
In June the bill went through a hearing and two subcommittee markups and was forwarded to the full Judiciary Committee, amended, by voice vote.
On August 5 the full committee approved the amended bill on a 17-12 vote; it was formally reported on September 10 and placed on the Union Calendar, the list of bills ready for floor action.

The amendments reported out softened the bill considerably from its introduced form, adding protections to keep small and same-state cases in state court, exempting securities class actions, preserving deadlines for plaintiffs on remand, and ordering a study of the effect on federal court workloads.
On October 1, 1998, the Rules Committee reported a rule (H. Res. 560) allowing one hour of debate with open amendments — the step right before a floor vote.
The House never took up the bill. When the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, it died on the calendar.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporate defendants facing class actions, and their insurers: state courts kept jurisdiction over consumer class actions for the time being. The idea did not die permanently — a similar bill, the Class Action Fairness Act, became law in 2005 and moved these cases to federal court after all.

sides.party_line_note: The committee vote was 17-12 with opposition concentrated among committee Democrats, and cosponsors were 8 Republicans and 2 Democrats — though one Democrat, Rep. Barney Frank of Massachusetts, added his sponsorship at reporting.

industries.note: Insurers are frequent defendants in policyholder and consumer class actions filed in state courts. The bill would have let them move those cases to federal court, where classes are harder to certify and cases more often dismissed.

Defective-product and drug-injury class actions are typically filed in state courts seen as friendlier to plaintiffs. Shifting them to federal court would have cut both certification rates and settlement pressure on companies like tobacco, auto, and pharmaceutical makers.
Hidden-fee and lending class actions usually start in state court. Broad removal rights would let lenders pull those cases to federal court, where they face longer odds.

The bill carved out class actions under the Securities Act of 1933 and cases about issuer communications to shareholders, leaving securities defendants' state-court exposure largely untouched even as other industries won relief.
State-court class certification is the backbone of this bar's practice; broad removal rights would have shrunk it sharply. Their interest in this bill ran with the consumers they represent.
